summary: Describes how to set up secure media connections over TLS using the Session Description Protocol. It defines the TCP/TLS protocol identifier and a fingerprint attribute that names the certificate the other side will present. It clarifies how multiple fingerprints are used. It replaces RFC 4572.

plainLanguage.summary: SDP can describe a media connection that uses TLS over TCP. It can also carry a fingerprint that lets the other endpoint check the certificate, provided the session description itself is protected.

subtitle: How SDP describes TLS media connections and verifies certificates with fingerprints.

tldr.problem: Endpoints that negotiate media sessions with SDP may need TLS, but often cannot obtain certificates signed by a well-known certification authority.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the SDP identifier TCP/TLS and a fingerprint attribute containing a secure hash of the certificate expected during the TLS handshake.
tldr.outcome: The fingerprint can authenticate a self-signed certificate only when the SDP description is protected against modification. RFC 8122 obsoletes RFC 4572 and is updated by RFC 8844.

today: RFC 8122 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2017. It obsoletes RFC 4572 and has been updated by RFC 8844.

sections.title: Using TLS for Media Sessions
sections.content:
The Session Description Protocol (SDP) describes multimedia sessions. RFC 4145 defines connection-oriented media over TCP; RFC 8122 extends that mechanism to TLS over TCP so a media stream can have confidentiality, integrity and authentication.

Endpoints may not have certificates signed by a well-known certification authority. They may have dynamic addresses and host names, and obtaining a signed certificate can require cost and administrative work. RFC 8122 lets an endpoint include a secure hash of its certificate, called a fingerprint, in the SDP description.

If the certificate presented in the TLS handshake matches the fingerprint, the endpoint can accept a self-signed certificate. This depends on the SDP description being protected against modification.
sections.plainLanguage: SDP can describe media carried over TLS and can include a hash of the expected certificate. The hash helps verify a self-signed certificate only if an attacker cannot change the SDP description.

sections.title: Session Modes and Threats
sections.content:
SDP is used in advertised mode, where a server publishes a session description, and offer-answer mode, where two participants negotiate descriptions. SIP uses offer-answer mode. The mode affects how the endpoints establish and check each other's identity.

TLS can protect a media stream from passive listeners and can authenticate endpoints against an attacker who sends traffic but cannot change the SDP. It cannot protect a session if an attacker can modify or redirect the session descriptions. The application protocol carrying SDP must provide integrity protection, for example through S/MIME in SIP.

When two endpoints have no prior relationship, a self-signed certificate is not trustworthy by itself. A protected SDP description can establish that relationship by carrying the certificate fingerprint.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS can protect media and verify a certificate, but it cannot protect an SDP description that an attacker can rewrite. The protocol carrying SDP must protect the description itself.

sections.title: TCP/TLS and Fingerprint Syntax
sections.content:
The SDP m line uses the protocol identifier TCP/TLS for TLS over TCP. It identifies only the transport, so the line must also identify the application format. Sessions use the setup and connection attributes defined by RFC 4145.

An endpoint MUST provide a certificate fingerprint. It is a secure one-way hash of the DER-encoded X.509 certificate. SDP writes the hash-function name followed by uppercase hexadecimal bytes separated by colons. A fingerprint can apply to a whole session or to one media description.

SHA-256 is the preferred hash. Implementations MUST NOT calculate or verify fingerprints with MD2 or MD5; those names remain listed so implementations can recognize them.
sections.plainLanguage: The fingerprint identifies a certificate by its hash, written in a standard SDP format. SHA-256 is preferred, and MD2 and MD5 must not be used to calculate or verify fingerprints.

sections.title: Choosing Among Multiple Fingerprints
sections.content:
An SDP media line may carry several fingerprints. They can be hashes of one certificate made with different functions, or hashes for multiple certificates that might be used for the media connection.

For each possible certificate, an endpoint must normally include a SHA-256 fingerprint and a fingerprint using the hash function used for the certificate's signature. The receiver selects the most preferred hash function available in the offer and checks each certificate against a fingerprint made with that function. If a certificate matches none of the selected fingerprints, the endpoint MUST NOT establish TLS.

The fingerprint attribute does not point to a specific certificate. The endpoint compares the presented certificate's hash against the offered values.
sections.plainLanguage: An SDP description may list several certificate hashes. The receiver chooses its preferred supported hash and refuses the connection if the certificate does not match.

sections.title: Checking the Certificate Identity
sections.content:
If the SDP description has integrity protection, the certificate may assert any syntactically valid identity. Without that protection, the certificate must identify the connection address or the endpoint that created the SDP, using the matching rules for IP addresses, DNS names or URIs.

The TLS server always presents a certificate. In offer-answer mode, the client also presents one, and the server requests it. If a presented certificate does not match an SDP fingerprint, the receiving endpoint ends the connection with a bad_certificate error.

An endpoint that starts listening before receiving the answer must not treat media data as valid until it receives a matching fingerprint in the answer. For advertised sessions without offer-answer, the server may request a client certificate or allow a client without one.
sections.plainLanguage: Both endpoints check certificates against the fingerprints in SDP. If a certificate does not match, the endpoint closes the media connection.

sections.title: Protecting the Session Description
sections.content:
A correct fingerprint does not remove the need for normal TLS negotiation. The endpoint still checks that the negotiated cipher and message-authentication method meet the application's needs. The RFC says an offered TLS_NULL_WITH_NULL_NULL cipher should be rejected in almost every scenario.

The application protocol carrying SDP is responsible for its integrity and should provide strong message authentication and replay protection. If it cannot, endpoints should remember certificates seen before, notify users about an unsecured certificate from a new party when possible, and warn strongly when a known party presents a different certificate.

Hop-by-hop protection such as SIPS may protect each network connection while leaving the description vulnerable to a compromised middlebox. RFC 8122 updates the preferred hash from SHA-1 to SHA-256 and clarifies the use of multiple fingerprints.
sections.plainLanguage: The fingerprint is useful only if the description carrying it cannot be changed without detection. Endpoints should check changes in certificates and warn users when the description is not protected end to end.
